title: The recovery research room
subtitle: Investigate a pattern, check a source, publish an honest briefing
objective: Use supplied sources and repeated sample data to present a cautious explanation of heart-rate recovery.

sow.exactOutcome: Research and present a healthy-body investigation.
sow.alignment: Directly develops this stated outcome with secondary-age tasks at an upper-KS2 conceptual level. Support and stretch are flexible; this exemplar is not a claim of qualification approval.

priorLearning: Read a table and subtract two whole numbers.
Distinguish a supported claim from a guarantee.
success: Select a relevant source and extract a useful scientific idea.
Describe a pattern using values from repeated data.
Present a claim, evidence, explanation and limitation without ranking health.

vocabulary.meaning: The number of heartbeats per minute.
The period after an activity while body responses move back towards a resting state.
Another trial using the same planned method.
The total of the values divided by the number of values.
A reason to restrict how far a conclusion can reach.

equipment: Shared evidence and source summaries, selected route, pencils, optional calculator.
preparation: Make clear that every number is constructed sample data, not a pupil or actual volunteer record.
No physical trial or online research is required. Print page 1 and the selected route.
safety: No exercise challenge, pulse measurement or comparison of pupils’ bodies.
Do not interpret the fictional rates as diagnosis, fitness rankings or age-specific normal limits.
If adapting to a later real practical, the school must plan it separately for individual access and relevant health needs. This pack supplies a complete paper route.
practicalAlternative: Analyse supplied constructed records and paraphrased primary-source summaries. Present as a paper research briefing; no actual trial is needed.

misconceptions.claim: A single rate proves how healthy somebody is.
misconceptions.correction: Many influences affect heart rate; this dataset cannot diagnose or rank health.
misconceptions.check: Ask what the records tell us and what they leave unknown.

misconceptions.claim: One repeat must exactly match the others.
misconceptions.correction: Repeated measurements can vary; variation helps us judge confidence.

misconceptions.claim: A source about general benefits proves this small trial’s conclusion.
misconceptions.correction: A relevant source can explain a pattern but does not turn constructed sample data into a real study.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether source statements and the sample measurements are the same kind of evidence.

access.supported: Read one trial; choose a relevant source and use a briefing frame.
access.stretch: Calculate selected means and evaluate a causal overclaim and test design.
access.regulation: Offer quiet pointing, private writing, drawing or adult scribing. Pass-and-return for public questions. Use fictional cases; no personal medical disclosure or comparison of bodies. Assign response routes from current evidence, not fixed pupil labels.

sources.title: NHLBI: How the heart beats
sources.note: Checked September 2026. During exercise heart rate usually increases to support oxygen delivery. No adult normal-range figures are applied to pupils.

sources.title: NHS: Physical activity for children and young people
sources.note: Checked September 2026. General activity context; the classroom investigates supplied constructed data, not pupils’ fitness or medical status.

sources.title: Department for Education: Science programmes of study
sources.note: Working-scientifically framing: evidence, reporting and conclusions. Activities are original and follow the user’s SoW.

slides.title: Can we publish this headline?
body: “One pulse number reveals perfect health.”
Your research team must check the evidence.
slides.notes: Introduce a research briefing with no real pupil data. Pupils may challenge a headline without challenging another pupil’s body or habits.

slides.title: Find the useful science
body: R1. What does the heart pump?
R2. Why might working muscles need more oxygen?
R3. Which is a number with a unit: “fast” or “96 beats/min”?
slides.notes: R1: blood. R2: working muscles have increased energy needs during activity and usually need more oxygen delivery. Accept “muscles working harder”. R3: 96 beats per minute is a measurement with a unit; “fast” lacks a numerical reference.

slides.title: I check what was compared
body: I read the method before the numbers.
The trials use the same planned conditions.
The numbers are a constructed classroom dataset.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I cannot claim we measured classmates. The comparison represents one fictional person with three repeat trials. Set recovery times help comparison. The same activity and duration matter. Equal starting values were built into this dataset; real trials may have different starting values.

slides.title: I describe a pattern using values
body: Trial A: 120 immediately after activity.
One minute later: 96. Two minutes later: 80.
I say “fell towards 72”, not “fully recovered”.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Think aloud: 120 − 96 = 24 beats per minute, the fall during the first minute. After two minutes, 80 remains 8 above the starting 72. The graph joins sample points to show a trend, not every measurement between them. This constructed pattern is consistent with recovery; it is not clinical proof.

visual.title: Trial A recovery graph
visual.description: Constructed sample line graph. Time after activity: 0 minutes, 120 beats per minute; 1 minute, 96; 2 minutes, 80. Vertical axis starts at zero. Resting value before trial: 72.

elements.text: Constructed sample data. Resting value before trial A: 72.

slides.title: I check repeats before a headline
body: Immediate values vary: 120, 116, 124.
Similar repeats strengthen a pattern description.
A mean summarises; it does not diagnose health.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Model the mean: the total is 360, divided by 3 trials gives 120 beats per minute. In real trials, variation may reflect biological differences or measurement differences. These constructed values illustrate that idea. Do not delete 116 or 124 simply because they differ.

visual.title: Repeated immediate heart rates
visual.description: Three zero-baseline bars show constructed immediate rates A 120, B 116, C 124 beats per minute. The mean is 120. Different trials can vary without one automatically being wrong.

elements.text: Immediate heart rate / beats per minute

Constructed sample repeats. Same planned method.
Mean = (120 + 116 + 124) ÷ 3 = 120.

slides.title: Evidence desk: find the pattern
body: Use the table and source cards on page 1.
W1. Describe the pattern in all three trials.
Use two values and name the units.
slides.notes: All trials show a fall during recovery: A from 120 to 80; B from 116 to 76; C from 124 to 84 beats per minute over two minutes. Each final rate remains above the starting 72. Pupils choose a pair and explain the pattern. No physical exercise is needed.

table.caption: Constructed sample data only. All rates are beats per minute.

slides.title: Which source helps explain it?
body: W2. Compare source A, B and C.
Choose one most directly relevant to heart-rate change.
Explain what the source cannot establish.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Source A is most directly relevant to oxygen delivery and heart-rate change. Source B provides broader activity context. Source C is an unattributed, unsupported absolute claim. The sources cannot prove that a constructed dataset came from a real trial or diagnose a person’s health.

slides.title: Write a better research headline
body: W3. Repair: “The fastest recovery proves the healthiest person.”
Use “in these sample trials” and a limitation.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Only one fictional person is represented; A, B and C are repeat trials, not three people. Model: In these sample trials, rates fell towards the starting value after activity. This cannot rank health or prove fitness.
slides.reveal: In these sample trials, heart rate fell during recovery. These records cannot rank health.

slides.title: A, B and C are three trials
body: Which conclusion matches the dataset?
slides.notes: A is incorrect: these are three trials for one fictional person, not three people. B is the correct bounded pattern. C is incorrect: 80, 76 and 84 remain above 72. Revisit the labels before independent work.

options.text: Person B must be healthier than person A.
options.feedback: A and B label trials, not different people. Rates alone cannot rank health.

options.text: All three sample trials show heart rate falling during recovery.
options.feedback: Each trial falls from its immediate value towards its starting value.

options.text: Every trial is back to 72 after two minutes.
options.feedback: The final values are 80, 76 and 84, all above 72.

slides.title: Prepare the research briefing
body: Choose one response route.
Include claim, evidence, explanation and limit.
Credit source A or B by organisation.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across You do. Pupils use the supplied sources; no online access is needed. The briefing can be a paper panel, typed paragraph or dictated 60-second script.

slides.title: Use the reporting frame
body: “The sample data show …”
“For example … beats per minute.”
“NHLBI explains … ; we cannot conclude …”
slides.notes: Shared You do time. The supported route uses trial A and source A. The standard route compares repeats. The stretch route calculates means and evaluates controls and causal claims.

slides.title: Check your headline
body: Are A, B and C labelled as trials?
Have I kept units and sample-data label?
Have I avoided a diagnosis or fitness ranking?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Require a constructed-data label near any chart or table pupils create. Do not accept faster recovery as proof of better health.

slides.title: Research editor check
body: Show one claim and its numerical evidence.
Ask whether the limit is clear.
Improve the headline before sharing.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. A teacher or private check can replace peer review. Specific feedback: include values and units; distinguish a source explanation from an actual measurement.

slides.title: Choose the next evidence question
body: Which would help: more repeats or an unsupported advert?
Propose one precise improvement to the method.
slides.notes: Lundy: collect proposals and explain which method detail would be added to the next paper dataset. Accept more repeats, longer recovery recording, standardised timing or a clearer measurement method. This does not authorise an unplanned physical trial.

slides.title: An honest research result
body: E1. Give one pattern with two values.
E2. Name the relevant source organisation.
E3. Give one limit to the conclusion.
slides.notes: E1: for example, trial A fell from 120 to 80 beats per minute over two minutes. E2: NHLBI for the heart-rate explanation. E3: constructed data for one fictional person cannot rank health. E4 on the pupil page asks for one control and its purpose.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: the research room
pupilPages.intro: All numbers are constructed sample data. A, B and C are repeat trials for one fictional person. Rates are beats per minute.

cards.title: Source A • NHLBI
cards.text: During activity, heart rate usually rises to help supply working muscles with more oxygen. This can explain a response; it does not diagnose a person.

cards.title: Source B • NHS
cards.text: Regular suitable physical activity can support health. This is broad guidance, not proof that a particular short trial measures total health.

cards.title: Source C • Unattributed advert
cards.text: “One pulse number tells you exactly who is healthiest.” No author, method or supporting evidence is supplied. This is a fictional claim for evaluation.

cards.title: Constructed method
cards.text: One fictional participant; three separate trials using the same activity, duration, room, recovery posture and measurement schedule. No class trial took place.

blocks.prompt: W1. Describe the common recovery pattern with two values and units.
W2. Which source best explains heart-rate change? Why? W3. Repair the “healthiest person” headline.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: one clear briefing
pupilPages.intro: Use trial A and source A on page 1.

blocks.prompt: S1. What do A, B and C label?
S2. Complete: Trial A fell from ____ to ____ beats per minute over two recovery minutes.
S3. Is 80 the same as the starting 72?
choices: Yes: fully back to the starting value
No: still above the starting value

blocks.prompt: S4. Complete: NHLBI explains that during activity the heart can beat faster to supply muscles with more ____ .
S5. Write or dictate a 3-sentence briefing: pattern; numbers; one thing the sample cannot prove.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: evidence-led briefing
pupilPages.intro: Use the whole dataset and source cards.

blocks.prompt: N1. Describe the common pattern across A–C. Use two pairs of values and units.
N2. Calculate the fall in trial A during the first minute. Show the subtraction.
N3. Choose the most relevant source for the heart-rate explanation. Explain why the advert is weak evidence.
N4. Write a short briefing with claim, evidence, scientific explanation and one limit.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: audit the research claim
pupilPages.intro: Keep constructed data separate from real observations and general source information.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate the mean immediate rate and mean rate after 1 minute. Show your working and units.
T2. Compare these means. Does this prove the same fall occurs for every person? Explain.
T3. Identify two controls in the method and one useful improvement. Explain their purposes.
T4. Write a cautious research headline and a 3-sentence briefing. Reject the claim that these data rank three people’s health.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Give precise evidence, not a diagnosis.

blocks.prompt: E1. Give one recovery pattern using two values and units.
E2. Name a relevant source organisation and the idea it supports.
E3. Give one limit to what these records can establish.
E4. Name one condition kept the same between trials and explain why.
Reflection. What should the next paper dataset investigate?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1: blood. R2: working muscles need more energy released in respiration, usually requiring more oxygen delivery. R3: 96 beats per minute is a measurement with units.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1: all trials fall towards 72: A 120→80, B 116→76 and C 124→84 beats per minute from immediately after activity to two minutes later. Final values remain above 72. W2: source A, NHLBI, directly explains heart-rate response and oxygen demand; B provides general context; C lacks attribution, method and supporting evidence. W3: make a bounded claim about sample trials, not a health ranking. A, B and C are repeats for one fictional person.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A is incorrect: trial labels are not people and rates cannot rank health. B is correct: each trial shows a fall during recovery. C is incorrect: 80, 76 and 84 are not equal to 72.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1: three repeat trials. S2: 120 to 80 beats per minute. S3: no, 80 is still above 72. S4: oxygen. S5 example: In this sample trial, heart rate fell during recovery. Trial A fell from 120 to 80 beats per minute over two minutes. These constructed records cannot diagnose or prove overall health.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1: appropriate pairs from any two trials, showing a common fall but not a return to 72. N2: 120 − 96 = 24 beats per minute. N3: source A, NHLBI; the advert has no author, method or supporting evidence and overclaims what one value can show. N4: bounded claim, accurate values and units, an oxygen-delivery explanation credited to NHLBI, and a limit such as constructed data, one fictional person, few repeats or limited recovery times.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1: immediate mean = (120 + 116 + 124) ÷ 3 = 120 beats per minute; one-minute mean = (96 + 92 + 100) ÷ 3 = 96 beats per minute. T2: the mean falls by 24 beats per minute. This does not establish a universal response, especially from constructed data for one person. T3: any two controls among activity, duration, room, recovery posture and measurement timing or method; each reduces an avoidable comparison difference. A useful improvement is more trials to explore variation, longer follow-up, or a clearer standardised measurement procedure. T4: report three sample trials for one fictional person, an accurate recovery pattern, numerical evidence, explanation and a limit.

answers.label: E1–E4 / reflection
answers.answer: E1: accurate paired values and units. E2: NHLBI for the heart-rate and oxygen-delivery explanation; NHS is acceptable for broad activity context if relevance is clear. E3: no clinical diagnosis, health ranking, claim of real measurement or universal conclusion. E4: one genuine control with an explanation of its comparison purpose. Reflection accepts a precise question for the next paper dataset.

answers.label: Assessment and re-teach
answers.answer: Secure: uses accurate values and units, identifies a relevant source, explains a heart-rate response and states an appropriate limit. If a health ranking appears, circle the trial labels and ask how many people are represented. If a pattern lacks numbers, require one paired comparison. If a mean is confused with a total, model total divided by number of trials.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.

The research task is self-contained: pupils compare primary-source summaries, analyse constructed data and present findings. It meets the SoW’s research/presentation focus without requiring internet accounts or any physical experiment.
All timing, rates and repeat methods are authored examples. They are not a recommended exercise prescription and not age-specific clinical reference values.
Interactive predictions map to the paper method/data/source tasks W1–W3. A pupil can test the claim by tracing the printed table and explaining the same conclusion.

interactive.title: Research room: prediction, data and a limit
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.

choices.text: Change the activity and timings every trial.
choices.feedback: Then differences could come from several changed conditions.
